list.listitem: Huntington disease (HD) is an inherited progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by choreiform movements, dystonia, psychiatric problems, and dementia. C
HD affects 5 to 10 per 100,000 of the general population in most Western European countries, as well as in the United States and Canada, with a lower prevalence in non-European ethnic groups. B
Expansion of the cytosine-adenine-guanine (CAG) repeat number over successive generations may cause an earlier and more severe phenotype (a phenomenon called anticipation). B
HD is characterized by the insidious onset of uncontrolled movements, loss of intellectual faculties, and emotional disturbance. B
Radiological findings on CT scan or MRI prominently show atrophy in the caudate and putamen. B
Treatment is limited to symptom management and optimizing quality of life. C

background.definition: Huntington disease (HD) is a progressive neurodegenerative genetic disorder that results from genetically programmed degeneration of neurons (in caudate and putamen) causing uncontrolled movements, loss of intellectual faculties, and emotional disturbance.

list.listitem: HD affects 5 to 10 per 100,000 white individuals, with a lower prevalence in non-European ethnic groups.
The incidence of HD is 0.38 per 100,00 per year.
HD is inherited in an autosomal dominant mode. HD is caused by an inherited unstable CAG triplet expansion on chromosome 4p16.3 that lengthens a polyglutamine segment in huntingtin protein.
CAG triplet repeats demonstrate somatic and germline instability causing expansion over successive generations.
This may cause earlier disease onset and a progressive worsening of the phenotype in subsequent generations, a phenomenon termed anticipation.
Huntingtin plays a role in protein trafficking, vesicle transport, postsynaptic signaling, transcriptional regulation, and apoptosis.
Pathology involves neuronal cell loss and atrophy of the caudate and putamen and generalized brain atrophy and loss of cerebellar Purkinje cells.

Genetic testing is potentially useful in embryos and for diagnostic or confirmatory testing in at-risk individuals or family members without symptoms of HD, to define the risk for the disease in their offspring. C
The diagnosis of HD relies on presence of the typical clinical features, a family history of the disease, and confirmatory genetic testing. C
Neuroimaging by CT or MRI helps to establish a preclinical diagnosis of HD. B
Clinically, HD is characterized by chorea, psychiatric illness, and dementia.
The most common presenting symptom of HD in adults is chorea.
Other usual findings at presentation include memory deficits, affective disturbances, personality changes, and other manifestations of motor dysfunction such as Parkinsonism and dystonia.
A hallmark of HD is unintended weight loss, likely the result of a hypermetabolic state.
A diagnosis given before a patient is 20 years of age is considered juvenile HD, in which chorea is notably absent. Children also have a more rapidly progressive disease.

Genetic testing: CAG trinucleotide expansion is the molecular basis of Huntington disease worldwide and is a highly sensitive and specific marker for inheritance of the disease mutation (sensitivity = 98%; specificity = 100%; LR+ = 99; LR− = 0.012). Genetic testing, as diagnostic or confirmatory testing, is indicated for individuals for whom you have a strong clinical suspicion of HD, with or without a family history.

Neuroimaging studies: Caudate atrophy can often be detected on brain imaging with CT scan or MRI. Caudate and putamen volume measurements by MRI suggest that striatal atrophy begins 9 to 20 years before the clinical diagnosis of HD.
Neuroimaging studies are not useful in early disease stages but are used for confirmation and differentiation of HD from other choreiform syndromes.
Axial MRI images through the lateral ventricles demonstrate typical and prominent findings of caudate atrophy in late-stage HD
A diagnosis of HD is based on the presence of typical clinical features and a family history of the disease.
Genetic testing should be performed in individuals for whom you have a strong clinical suspicion of HD, with or without a family history.
Treatment is largely supportive.
Treatment is limited to symptom management and optimizing quality of life by an interdisciplinary team approach. C
Pharmacological treatment with tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine, neuroleptics (typical and atypical), and amantadine are of some proven value. B
As there is no known cure, treatment is symptomatic and remains supportive.

Three classes of medications are commonly used to suppress chorea in Huntington disease: neuroleptics, such as haloperidol and fluphenazine; benzodiazepines, such as clonazepam and diazepam; and dopamine-depleting agents, such as reserpine and tetrabenazine (TBZ).
The American Academy of Neurology's evidence-based pharmacological guideline for chorea recommends tetrabenazine (up to 100 mg/d), or amantadine (300-400 mg/d) or riluzole (200 mg/d).

TBZ effectively suppresses HD-related chorea for up to 80 weeks. Patients treated chronically with TBZ should be monitored for parkinsonism, dysphagia, and other side effects including sleep disturbance, depression, anxiety, and akathisia.
The combination of TBZ and a neuroleptic agent may occasionally be beneficial if chorea is very severe and unresponsive to monotherapy with neuroleptics.

Deutetrabenazine has been assessed in a randomized clinical trial. This is a molecule of tetrabenazine in which hydrogen molecules have been substituted for deuterium (a non-toxic form of hydrogen that froms a stronger bond with carbon and is thus less prone to metabolism). Among 90 patients with HD (mean age 53.7 years) deutetrabenazine was associated with improved motor signs at 12 weeks.
Rigidity and bradykinesia in HD generally do not require treatment.
Short-term administration of latrepirdine is well tolerated in patients with HD but does not improve cognition or global functioning.
Depression is a common symptom of HD and is usually managed with tricyclic antidepressants or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.
Ethyl-eicosapentaenoic acid was found to be no better than placebo at improving motor function in patients with HD.
Creatine (up to 40 mg/d) is not associated with a delay in functional decline in patients with HD.
Coenzyme Q10 is not associated with a delay in functional decline in patients with HD.
The role of chronic bilateral deep brain stimulation in improvement of choreiform movements warrants further study.
A high-calorie diet is usually necessary to compensate for dysphagia and high metabolic needs (involuntary movements); consultation with a dietician should be considered to prevent weight loss.
The natural history of the cardinal features of HD include declines in movement, cognition, behavior and functions.

With disease progression, motor function slowly deteriorates over 10 to 30 years and leads to significant morbidity and early mortality; dysphagia and aspiration pneumonia are common causes of death. C
The rate of deterioration in cognitive and motor dysfunction predicts morbidity and early mortality. C
End-of-life issues should be discussed with the patient and family before cognitive and motor impairment become severe. C
